chapter_theme: The chapter gathers counsel on the household and the realm: which women a man avoids and which men guard a woman, a wife's excellence and her hold on her husband, the farmer's care and ruin, the fortress and the minister, and the rewards of learning; several verses on women and marriage state period norms of gender and astrology.

41.reading: The verse names five women whom men who know keep away from, recoiling as from an enemy: a girl not yet come of age, a woman past her menses, a woman bearing the sign of renunciation, a woman who at no time guards herself, and any other man's wife.
41.nuance: The list widens the Kural's single prohibition (another's wife) into a set of women barred by age, bodily state, vow and conduct. இலிங்கி is a woman who bears an ascetic's sign; ஓவாதான் கோலம் on line 2 may describe her garb ('the dress of one who never leaves it'), and the division of line 2 is our construal.

items.claim: a girl who has not yet come of age is one of the five men avoid
a woman whose menses have ended is one of the five men avoid
a woman bearing the sign of renunciation, in its unbroken garb, is one of the five men avoid
a woman who at no time guards herself is one of the five men avoid
whoever is another man's wife is one of the five men avoid

norm.note: a rule of the period on which women a man may approach, set by age, menses, vow and marriage

42.reading: The verse says a woman's excellence lies in knowing the household's ways in proportion to its income, not angering kin, eagerly tending guests, and always worshipping, with a clear mind, the one who brings her fortune and the gods.
42.nuance: திருவாக்கும் is read here as the one who makes her fortune, most likely the husband, so worship is owed both to him and to the deity; if it qualifies தெய்வதை instead, the list has four items. Income comes first, as in the Kural's definition of the wife.

items.claim: knowing the household's ways in proportion to its income is a wife's excellence
not angering the kin is a wife's excellence
tending guests with eagerness is a wife's excellence
worshipping the one who brings her fortune is a wife's excellence
worshipping the deity always, with a clear mind, is a wife's excellence

norm.note: a period norm defining a wife's excellence by household management, hospitality and worship

43.reading: The verse says that if one finds a man who knows the five (the agreement of birth-stars, the auspicious hour, the agreement of planets, the yoga and the qualities) and whether the couple are fit to be joined, one should have him fix the wedding day.
43.domain_note: fixing the day of a marriage
43.nuance: Astrology is given here as a learned craft with five parts, and the counsel is to seek out its expert. தோள்கூட்டல் உற்றானும் அல்லானும் ('one fit and not fit for the joining of shoulders') is read as the reckoning of the couple's match; it could also mean the bridegroom and others.

items.claim: the agreement of the couple's birth-stars is one of the five the reckoner must know
the auspicious hour is one of the five
the agreement of the planets is one of the five
the yoga of the day is one of the five
the qualities are one of the five

norm.note: a ritual rule of the period: the wedding day is fixed by astrological reckoning

44.reading: The verse names five qualities (guarded restraint, a greatness that does not covet, dignity, modesty and reserve) and says a woman without them, even if she were Lakshmi herself with jewelled breasts like kongu buds on a golden hill, is hard to bring within one's bounds.
44.domain_note: a wife, as the husband sees her
44.nuance: நாண்ஒடுக்கம் is split into two to reach the count; read as one, there are four. The verse ranks the five above beauty at its divine limit, but its measure is whether the husband can hold her, not her own good.

items.claim: guarded restraint is one of the five without which a woman cannot be held
a greatness that does not covet is one of the five
dignity is one of the five
modesty is one of the five
reserve is one of the five

norm.note: a period norm on the qualities that keep a wife within her husband's bounds

45.reading: Addressing a long-haired woman, the verse traces a chain the world repeats without end: as the ridge of the field rises the water rises, as the water rises the paddy rises, as the paddy rises the undiminished people rise, and as the people rise the king rises.
45.nuance: Each item is the cause of the next, so the list is a ladder, not a set: the king's height is the last effect of a field bank. ஓவா(து) உரைக்கும் உலகு gives it as a common saying.

items.claim: the ridge of the field rising lifts the water
the water rising lifts the paddy
the paddy rising lifts the people
the undiminished people rising lifts the king
the king rises last, as the effect of all the rest

46.reading: The verse names the conduct of a good house: wasting nothing, raising up those who depend on it, blaming no one, sharing with everyone without hiding, and not milking so that the calf dies.
46.nuance: The calf whose milk is taken is set in the same list as dependants and guests, so the house's care reaches its animals. The closing மன்றுசார் வாசு மனை is obscure; we take it as praise of such a house before the common ground, and எத்துவமும் as 'anything at all'.

items.claim: wasting nothing at all marks a good house
raising up those who depend on it marks a good house
blaming no one marks a good house
sharing with everyone, without hiding anything, marks a good house
not milking the cow so that its calf dies marks a good house

47.reading: Addressing a woman, the verse says those who understand well never kill the hope of those who long for them, the meal of their kin, their own generosity or their fame, and will not consent to kill whatever they might gain by it.
47.nuance: The verse plays on கொல்: hope, a meal, generosity and fame are 'killed' by neglect, and the last 'killing' is the literal one, refused at any gain. The fifth killing has no object of its own in the Tamil, so we give four items and read the close as the frame.

items.claim: those who know do not kill the hope of those who long for them
they do not kill the meal of their kin
they do not kill their own generosity
they do not kill their fame

48.reading: The verse says the wise have examined five things as a fortress (deep water, forest, saline waste, a lofty hill reaching the sky, and the people) and that the rule is to establish as king the one who has them.

items.claim: deep water is one of the five defences
forest is one of the five defences
saline waste land is one of the five defences
a lofty hill reaching the sky is one of the five defences
the people are one of the five defences

49.reading: The verse names five ruins for the ploughman: negligence, pride in wealth, leaving work unfinished, quarrelling, and falling out with the skilled worker.
49.nuance: The last two ruins are social: a farmer is ruined by quarrels and by losing the craftsman he depends on, not only by his own sloth.

items.claim: negligence ruins the ploughman
pride in wealth ruins the ploughman
leaving work unfinished ruins the ploughman
quarrelling ruins the ploughman
falling out with the skilled worker ruins the ploughman

50.reading: The verse sets not killing as good and killing, not learning letters, and anger as bad, and calls a place where kin are wholly free of blame, without the good having to speak first, a town where many may live.
50.nuance: The first four items are verdicts of good and bad in the same breath, so illiteracy and anger are weighed on the scale of killing. The last two lines are hard to divide; we read them as the place where such conduct prevails.

items.claim: not killing is good
killing is bad
not learning letters is bad
anger is bad
where kin are wholly free of blame, without the good having to speak first, is a town for many

51.reading: The verse says fasting with desire put away is good, hosting guests without reckoning a return is good, and scorning the weak is bad, and that those who do not go to others' houses are rare and those who do not eat from others' hands are great.
51.nuance: The list joins the ascetic's fast and the householder's guest, then turns both into a pride of self-reliance: not entering others' houses, not eating from their hands.

items.claim: fasting is good when desire has been put away
hosting guests without reckoning a return is good
scorning the weak is bad
those who do not go to others' houses are rare
those who do not eat from others' hands become great

52.reading: The verse names the medicines by which women bring the husband to yield: bearing children, innocence, beauty, living with him in accord, restraint in food, and not being restless in speech.
52.nuance: The verse says ஐந்து but the Tamil yields six phrases; we give six, though மடனுடைமை மாதுடைமை may have been counted as one. The medicine works on the husband: the wife's virtues are named as her means of holding him.

items.claim: bearing children brings the husband to yield
innocence brings the husband to yield
beauty brings the husband to yield
living with him in accord brings him to yield
restraint in food brings him to yield
not being restless in speech brings him to yield

norm.note: a period norm naming a wife's qualities as means of holding her husband

53.reading: Addressing a garlanded man, the verse names the five who guard a well-adorned woman, when one considers it: the husband who took her, her brother, her maternal uncle, her son and her father.
53.domain_note: the men of a woman's family
53.nuance: கொண்டான் கொழுநன் is read as one person, the husband who took her, which gives five; read as two it gives six. Every guardian is a man of her family.

items.claim: the husband who took her is one of her five guardians
her brother is one of her guardians
her maternal uncle is one of her guardians
her son is one of her guardians
her father is one of her guardians

norm.note: a period norm placing a woman under the guard of the men of her family

54.reading: The verse says that if a woman lets her lily-red mouth, eyes, mind and long brows run many ways and does not guard her restraint, she is held like the bent-earringed dancer whom scorners make to perform on a tall bamboo pole.
54.nuance: The count word says five but four parts are named (mouth, eyes, mind, brows); a fifth may be lost or ஆம்பல் may have been counted apart. The guard here is her own நிறை, not a man's watch. The pole dancer of the close is our reading of an obscure image.

items.claim: a lily-red mouth that runs many ways loses a woman her restraint
eyes that run many ways
a mind that runs many ways
long brows that play many ways

norm.note: a period norm on a woman's guarding of her own glance, speech and mind

55.reading: The verse says the learned man wins gold, the good poet wealth and the debater fame, while the unlearned and those outside the company of the learned win only laughter among the good.
55.nuance: The rewards are graded by the kind of learning: gold, wealth, fame. என்பெறும் வாதி may be a question ('what does the debater gain? fame').

items.claim: the learned man wins gold
the good poet wins wealth
the debater wins fame
the unlearned win laughter among the good
those not of the learned's company win laughter among the good

56.reading: The verse calls it wisdom to bring the good to light, forget the bad, be quickly a staff of strength to living beings, turn deceit away from others' property, and, for a man of honour, to perish.
56.nuance: The list ends on a hard turn: after four acts of care and honesty, the fifth wise act is to die, and only for the man of honour (மானத்தான் ஆயின்).

items.claim: bringing the good to light is wisdom
forgetting the bad is wisdom
being quickly a staff of strength to living beings is wisdom
turning deceit away from others' property is wisdom
for a man of honour, perishing is wisdom

57.reading: The verse says the king's minister, with his great power to split anything open and know it, acts only after closely measuring his own position, the state of the work that must not fail, the state of the houses of those who oppose him in strength, and the matchless order of things.
57.nuance: The Tamil names four நிலை; the minister's own power in the last line may be the fifth root. We give four items.

items.claim: his own position is measured before he acts
the state of the work that must not fail is measured
the state of the houses of those who oppose him in strength is measured
the matchless order of things is measured

58.reading: The verse names five qualities (wealth, enjoyment, fearlessness, a grace that does not leave even at the hour of death, and rare dharma) and says the man who has them is the one a king of sharp spear can trust.

items.claim: wealth is a quality of the man the king trusts
enjoyment is a quality of the man the king trusts
fearlessness is a quality of the man the king trusts
a grace that does not leave even at the hour of death is a quality of the trusted man
rare dharma is a quality of the trusted man

59.reading: The verse says the farmer, in a good field, stores straw, tends the cattle daily, readies the small tools and tends the manure before he sets the fitted plough to the soil, and those who recite the texts hold a finer plough.
59.domain_note: the farmer, set beside the reciter of texts
59.nuance: The last line turns the farmer's labour into an image for study: the scholar's plough is the subtle one. Line 1 (மா டோ) and line 3 (என்றிலை) are doubtful, so the division is ours.

items.claim: storing the straw is part of the farmer's care
tending the cattle daily is part of his care
readying the small tools is part of his care
tending the manure is part of his care
the fitted plough is set to the field last

60.reading: The verse names five claims and says it has never yet seen anyone who makes them: that not receiving is good, that giving is bad, that falling short is good for those without character, that falling short is good even when learning fails, and that doing much penance is bad.
60.nuance: The division turns on sandhi (நன்றீதல் may be நன்று ஈதல்) and on how far என்பாரை reaches. The first claim sits oddly among absurdities, since refusing gifts is praised elsewhere; it may be read as 'refusing to give', or the closing may govern only the last claim.

items.claim: no one is seen saying that not receiving is good
no one is seen saying that giving is bad
no one is seen saying that falling short is good for those without character
no one is seen saying that falling short is good even when learning fails
no one is seen saying that doing much penance is bad

links.note: Kural 148 calls it manhood not to look at another's wife; verse 41 puts another's wife last in a list of five women men avoid.
links.teaches: The couplet's one rule becomes a whole map of forbidden women, so the Kural's virtue of restraint is turned into a period code drawn by age, menses and vow.
links.list_adds: It sets another's wife among a girl, a woman past her menses, a female ascetic and an unguarded woman, so adultery becomes one case of a wider bar by bodily state and vow.

links.note: Kural 55 praises the wife who does not worship a god but rises worshipping her husband; verse 42 counts worship of the deity, beside the one who brings her fortune, as part of a wife's excellence.
links.teaches: Read flatly, the Kural sets the husband in place of the god while this verse asks the wife to worship both, so the two works divide on whether her devotion may go beyond the house.
links.list_adds: It sets the deity's worship as a fifth duty beside income, kin and guests, making religion one household task among others rather than the one the husband displaces.

links.note: Kural 51 defines the wife by the home's excellence and living within her husband's means; verse 42 opens with knowing the house's ways in proportion to income.
links.teaches: Both works put income first in defining a wife, and the verse spells out what the couplet's 'excellence of the home' includes: kin kept content, guests and worship.
links.list_adds: It ranks budgeting first and then lists the duties it must pay for, so the couplet's measure of means becomes the base of a household order.

links.note: Verse 43 tells one to seek the man who knows five parts of astrology and have him fix the wedding day; Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest of fools.
links.teaches: Two Jain-era ethics works disagree on the worth of the same learned craft: one treats astrology as the expert's knowledge a marriage needs, the other as a madman's distraction from death.
links.list_adds: It breaks astrology into five technical parts, treating it as a craft to be mastered, which is exactly what the quatrain mocks as endless prattle.

links.note: Naladiyar 386 says beauty in a modest woman is like learning in the wise or a sword in a hero's hand; verse 44 says that without modesty and four other qualities even Lakshmi's beauty cannot be held.
links.teaches: The pair state one claim from both sides: modesty makes beauty serviceable, and beauty without it is ungovernable, so beauty in both works has worth only as the instrument of a virtue.
links.list_adds: It names four qualities beside modesty and sets them against beauty at its divine limit, a ranking the quatrain's three similes leave implicit.

links.note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the king's sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 45 says the king rises only as the field bank, water, paddy and people rise beneath him.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the people depend on the king, while the verse runs the dependence upward from a mud ridge, so read together they show the dependence runs both ways.
links.list_adds: Its chain of five causes puts the king at the end of a ladder of rises beginning with a field bank, a causal order the couplet does not trace.

links.note: Kural 1034 says farmers see many kings' umbrellas under their own; verse 45 traces a king's rise to the rising of the field's water and paddy.
links.teaches: The couplet's claim that farming underwrites kingship is given its mechanism: the height of the crown is measured from the height of the field bank.
links.list_adds: It sets out each link from field to throne in order, where the couplet states only the end result.

links.note: Kural 44 says a household that fears blame and shares its food never loses its line; verse 46 counts not blaming and sharing with all among the marks of a good house.
links.teaches: The couplet's two conditions of a lasting house reappear inside a longer list that adds care for dependants and for the calf, so the house's sharing is carried to its animals.
links.list_adds: It places sharing beside not milking a calf to death, so household generosity is extended to the livestock, which the couplet does not reach.

links.note: Kural 328 says gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy however great; verse 47 ends that those who know will not kill whatever they gain.
links.teaches: The verse takes the couplet's refusal of gain by killing and widens killing to the hope of the needy, the kin's meal, one's generosity and fame, so neglect becomes a kind of slaying.
links.list_adds: Its pun on கொல் puts killing a life beside killing a hope or a reputation, making non-killing a rule for social conduct as well as for life.

links.note: Kural 742 names water, open ground, hill and shady forest as a fort; verse 48 names deep water, forest, saline waste, a lofty hill and the people, and makes having them the rule for crowning a king.
links.teaches: The fort of the couplet gains a fifth wall made of people, and its possession becomes the test for who may be made king rather than a feature of a stronghold.
links.list_adds: It adds the people as a fifth defence and turns the list into a qualification for kingship, which the couplet's list of terrain does not do.

links.note: Thirikadugam 100 names a loyal army, a fearless fortress and great treasure as the limbs of kings; verse 48 breaks the fortress into five and makes it the ground of being crowned.
links.teaches: One counted work treats the fort as one limb among three, the other spells it out as five, with the people among them, so the two together show the fort as both a royal possession and a living defence.

links.note: Kural 1039 says land left by an owner who does not go to it sulks like a wife; verse 49 counts negligence first among five ruins of the ploughman.
links.teaches: The couplet's single fault of absence is set at the head of a list that adds pride, unfinished work, quarrels and a broken tie with the craftsman, so a farm fails socially as well as by neglect.
links.list_adds: It sets negligence among social and moral causes of ruin, where the couplet names absence alone.

links.note: Verse 12 calls killing and eating flesh poison among five poisons; verse 50 calls not killing good and killing bad, then weighs illiteracy and anger on the same scale.
links.teaches: Within the book, killing is the fixed first term of two lists, and in each the author sets lesser faults (overpowering the weak, slander, illiteracy, anger) beside it, so its scale of harms keeps killing as the measure.

links.note: Kural 211 says duty seeks no return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain; verse 51 calls it good to host guests without reckoning a return.
links.teaches: The couplet's principle of giving without return is carried to the guest at the door, and the verse sets it next to fasting and not eating from others' hands, so giving freely and taking nothing are one ideal.
links.list_adds: It pairs the host who expects no return with the man who will not eat from another's hand, so the list joins the giver's and the receiver's sides of the same refusal.

links.note: Kural 60 calls good children the ornament of a home's excellence; verse 52 counts bearing children first among a wife's medicines that make the husband yield.
links.teaches: Children, an ornament of the house in the couplet, become in the verse the wife's first hold over her husband, so the same good is read for its effect within the marriage.
links.list_adds: It sets childbearing beside beauty, accord and restraint in food as means of holding the husband, a use of children the couplet does not name.

links.note: Verse 44 names five qualities without which a woman cannot be held by her husband; verse 52 names six by which a wife holds him.
links.teaches: The two verses look at the same marriage from opposite ends: what lets a husband keep a wife within bounds and what lets a wife bring a husband to yield, so the book treats control as running both ways.

links.note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding by confinement is and puts a woman's own steadfastness first; verse 53 names five men of her family as the ones who guard her.
links.teaches: Read as a claim about what keeps a woman, the couplet moves the guard inside her while the verse places it in her husband, brother, uncle, son and father, so the two disagree on where chastity is kept.
links.list_adds: It names the guard as five kinsmen, a list of external keepers that the couplet's single inner guard sets aside.

links.note: Verse 53 names five kinsmen who guard a woman; verse 54 says she falls if she herself does not guard her restraint.
links.teaches: Placed side by side in the book, the two verses split the guard between the men of her family and her own நிறை, so the book holds both views the Kural sets against each other.

links.note: Naladiyar 139 says the unlearned who keep company with the learned gain sense daily; verse 55 says the unlearned who stay outside the learned's company gain only laughter.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the remedy and the verse gives the cost of refusing it, so together they make company, not learning alone, the line between gaining sense and being mocked.
links.list_adds: It grades rewards (gold, wealth, fame, laughter) by kind of learning and company, setting the unlearned at the bottom of a ladder the quatrain does not draw.

links.note: Kural 969 says men of honour give up life when honour is at stake, like the yak; verse 56 makes perishing, for the man of honour, the last of five acts of wisdom.
links.teaches: Death for honour, a matter of nature and pride in the couplet, is counted here as wisdom beside forgiveness and care for living beings, so it is framed as discernment rather than temper.
links.list_adds: It sets dying for honour beside revealing good, forgetting wrongs and helping living beings, so the list makes it one act of wisdom among gentler ones.

links.note: Kural 471 says to weigh the strength of the deed, oneself, the opponent and allies before acting; verse 57 says the minister acts after measuring his own state, the work, the opponents' state and the order of things.
links.teaches: The couplet's four-fold weighing is given to the minister and its fourth term changes from allies to the matchless order of things, so prudence moves from counting forces to reading circumstance.
links.list_adds: It moves the reckoning to the minister and replaces allies with the order of things, a different fourth term than the couplet's.

links.note: Kural 501 says a man is trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life; verse 58 says the trusted man has wealth, enjoyment, fearlessness, grace at death and rare dharma.
links.teaches: Where the couplet uses wealth, pleasure and fear as temptations to test a man, the verse treats wealth, enjoyment and fearlessness as qualities he must have, and adds grace, so the same terms change from tests to credentials.
links.list_adds: It turns the couplet's four tests into five possessions and adds grace that survives death, which the couplet does not name.

links.note: Kural 1038 ranks manuring above ploughing and guarding above watering; verse 59 lists storing straw, cattle, tools and manure as care that comes before the plough is set.
links.teaches: Both put the plough after other care, and the verse widens the couplet's ladder to the farmer's stores and animals, then turns the whole into an image for the scholar's finer plough.
links.list_adds: It sets manure among the farmer's other provisions and closes with the reciter of texts, so the farming list becomes a figure for study.

links.note: Verse 49 names five ruins of the ploughman; verse 59 names the care he gives before he ploughs.
links.teaches: The book gives the farmer's life as a pair of lists, what ruins him and what he must tend, so negligence in 49 is answered item by item by the provisions of 59.

source_issues: Verse 41 line 1: பூவாதான் with final ன் where the list of women needs பூவாதாள்; line 2 ஓவாதான் likewise.
Verse 54: the count word says five (என்றைந்தும்) but line 1 names four parts; a part may be lost.
Verse 52: the count word says ஐந்து but six phrases are listed.
Verse 59 line 1: நாளும்மா டோ போற்றிப் looks corrupt (perhaps மாடு ஓம்பி or மாடோம்பி); line 3 என்றிலை is obscure.
Verse 46 line 4: மன்றுசார் வாசு மனை is obscure; வாசு may be corrupt.
